title: Death.
html:
Several months ago I buried my grandfather. I know it’s a strange way to introduce a topic, but it felt fitting for a discussion on death. I preached a sermon at his funeral on the value of hope, but it struck me throughout the planning and lead up, how little we in the west actually come face to face with death, and how absurdly abnormal that is (historically speaking). My cousin remarked that she had never seen a casket in person. Early last year I did a 12 week intensive practicum working as an on-call chaplain for a major hospital. I was flung from the comfortable, naïve, western world, into one of the only places in our society that actually still confronts death head on, and it was an interesting experience to say the least. It’s hard to oversell just how averse to death we are as a society, but it’s no surprise really. Death is the ultimate absolute that spits in the face of a culture that pretends that absolutes don’t actually exist. Truth is subjective and reality is malleable, until death comes knocking.

Thanks for reading my Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

I operate from a Christ-centered worldview, so I imagine that my experiences and perspectives on death may strike some of you as odd. Death, for the Christian, is many things at once. It’s the culmination of a life lived, it’s a metaphor for how we are to live that life, it’s an end, and a beginning. It’s a gateway into a better tomorrow, and yet death itself is not to be desired, so much as what naturally follows it. That which lies on the other side. It represents an opportunity to join with the church throughout history, and to experience our relationship with God in a whole new way. Despite the generally positive nature of most of these attributes I have listed, I don’t want anyone to think that it lacks gravity, weight, and sadness. These things of course are still expected and natural, and certainly very familiar for me. Lamentations is the name of one of the books of the Bible, and it is essentially a book of mourning and grieving death, and suffering.

The culture at large has a very low view of death, probably because we’ve all become so desensitized to it (in certain contexts, but not in others). It’s strange to think about really; how many of you reading have ever seen a dead body in real life? Touched one? And yet, how many of us have watched horrible deaths actually occur in front of our eyes through some sort of screen? When Kirk was assassinated, how many people actually watched it happen on socials? We distance ourselves and become numb to the intensity of it, while also avoiding any actual confrontation with the reality of it. Backwards world.

I say all this because in many ways I view the world through the lens of tension and release; without tension, the release or resolution loses its meaning and importance. I think we have done the same thing with death and life. Because we cheapen the impact of death, we invariably cheapen the impact of life.

I remember early last year I had the privilege of attending the graduation of a group therapy sort of ministry at our church and I listened to the story of a mother (who is well known to me) talk about what brought her to that place. Her family had been through some pretty brutal suffering over the past few years, some of which I had witnessed and supported her son and daughter through. She talked about how the death of her young niece tore their family apart, and how she thought that would be the end of it, but somehow bad things just kept happening as the years wore on. She talked about how this all broke her down and required a choice from her; despair or God. This public declaration, after a long year of work, highlighted how beautiful life can be if we learn to accept our suffering. If we learn to make peace with death, something astounding happens. The tension in her life was resolved when she turned back towards her savior.

As I process my thoughts on death and write this, I am reminded of one of my favorite scenes in the Marvel Cinematic Universe; the scene between Vision and the final Ultron body. Ultron is about to die, and they have a short discussion on death and life and their respective meanings, and Vision says something profound; ‘a thing isn’t beautiful because it lasts’. A flower fades, a bird dies, one of the defining characteristics of life is that it changes, it moves, it pulls and pushes, and part of the reason why we assign the term ‘beautiful’ to it, is because of that fact. The fact that life cannot stay where it is.

To be frank, I do not know how to offer hope to those outside Christ. I personally have found no other rational source for optimism in this life other than the eternal security that is afforded to me as a result of submission to Jesus Christ. It is the reason I can look at the world and not be crushed by the weight of suffering and death. I do know, however, that viewing death in its proper place, as something which lends meaning to life, something which acts as the foil to life, is the best way of thinking about it that I have found.

Thanks for reading.

title: Gratitude.
html:
If there were ever one single practical tip I could give to people today, in order that they might live lives more satisfied and joyous, I would tell them to actively carve out moments in life to practice the virtue of gratitude. To recount even the smallest gifts they had been given, and to choose, in that moment, to be grateful for them. Unfortunately, in our consumer culture today, we no longer teach or encourage gratitude. Instead, as a collective, we focus incessantly on that which we do not have. This is why envy is one of the most silent soul killers, running rampant in the west today; gratitude and envy are opposites, if we fail to practice gratitude, it’s no wonder that envy abounds. Life becomes less about appreciating the incredible blessing each of us has, and more about eyeing hungrily that which someone else has. As I have said before, at a societal level, you get what you incentivize, and we are pouring social and financial incentives into the perpetuation of envy. A course correction is in order.

Thanks for reading Joshua's Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

What do you think would happen as a society if our people took time every day to briefly acknowledge the good things in their lives? If they chose to recognize and be grateful for that which they already have? If instead of chasing the next high, they sat for a moment and enjoyed what was already in front of them? Gratitude is quite difficult, I understand. It requires a measure of discipline, like any virtue. But its benefits outweigh the sacrifice. Any cursory examination of the evidence will clearly demonstrate a tie between one’s ability to be grateful, and one’s overall life satisfaction. If hope is that virtue which brings with it the greatest ability to change the future and drive us towards a better tomorrow, gratitude is that virtue which brings with it the greatest ability to appreciate today. Gratitude allows us to rest and refocus ourselves on the things that matter, keeping us from getting lost in a constant push for something else. It reminds us that each moment is a gift, and forces us to slow down when everything else in life says ‘go faster’.

So how do we do this? I’m a bible thumper, so when I have questions as such, I look to scripture;

“give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.”

I am not trying to sound trite when I say it really is that simple. In every circumstance in this life, there are opportunities to practice gratitude. Every circumstance. Sorry if that sounds too hardcore for you, but I mean it, and I try very hard (with varying levels of success) to implement it in my life, and have for many years now. I practice what I preach.

For illustrative purposes, however, I had a pretty nasty fever this weekend, and it was stark how much more difficult to be virtuous it was when my body felt so horrible. At the same time, however, it forced me to slow down some, to really stop and reflect on things in a new way. One thing that I realized is just what I said; it is immensely more difficult to be virtuous when my body feels horrible. Some might see this as an excuse; my body feels horrible, therefore practicing virtue is going to be hard, but the reality is that we actually have a substantial amount of ability to change how our body feels. This is why I keep telling people to exercise and eat healthy. In the process, you will need to build some discipline, and in doing so your body will begin to feel better overall, creating a sort of feedback loop, where the practice of virtue leads to easier practice of another, which leads to easier practice of another, until they start to become truly habitual responses to various external stimuli. Next thing you know, you’re a saint! I jest of course, but this feedback loop is seriously beneficial, despite being rather difficult to attain.

One thing that has helped me immensely in my own practice of gratitude is cigars. Not for everyone, I know, but the underlying idea is transferable. Cigars beget stillness. They require 45 to 90 mins of stillness. For me and many others, they represent a healthy solitude, to sit, to appreciate, and to fully exist in the moment. No distraction, just stillness. I have not found any other more effective means for generating gratitude in my life than lighting up a cigar, sitting out on my porch, watching the birds, and the sunset, and the smoke billowing away into the sky. All I can ever seem to do in those moments is thank God for an incomprehensibly good existence.

The point is this; find something that forces you to sit still for 1 hour a week. Sit somewhere beautiful, whether in nature, or somewhere with beautiful architecture. Do not even think about going on your phone. Seriously. Leave your phone in the house, or in your car, or something. Don’t bring a book, don’t go with someone else, just sit and watch the world around you. Perhaps this method won’t work for others, I don’t know, but these are the moments where my gratitude for life naturally bubbles out of me. I suppose calling it natural when it requires this much intentional effort may be a bit of a stretch, but I digress.

Gratitude is a choice, and it is a choice that is so often drowned among the waves of consumeristic distraction that wash over us on the daily. Fighting these waves is not easy, but it is necessary if we wish to advance forward, and heal from the cultural decay that rots away all around us. Each of us has the ability to choose to be thankful for that which we are blessed with. Do so, and do so often. Thanks for reading. As always, let me know what you think.

title: Charity.
html:
So this week I want to discuss the virtue of charity. Not the modern definition though, I am not referring to the practice of giving things away to those in need (a topic for another time), and I am also not referring to what we would today simply refer to as love. Rather I am interested in the practice of giving other people the benefit of the doubt. I suspect that if this script were ever to reach a substantial western population (doubtful it seems), I would promptly find myself accosted by many people refusing to give me any charity (that is, the benefit of the doubt). Since there will likely be both misunderstanding, and misrepresentation, allow me to define precisely what I am not advocating for; I am not advocating for a naïve, unlearned, careless approach to interacting with other people. I am not saying we should all just act as though everyone’s opinions are equal and valid and have merit. This is clearly not the case, and much of online rhetoric at the moment is people coming to terms with the fact that not all ideas are created equal. This is a good thing.

What I am saying, however, is that people on the internet need to relearn charity, that is, the ability to objectively look at what someone is saying (and not saying), and evaluate their words on the basis of the their merits, in a rational manner, without excessive emotion, and in a manner which fairly (or charitably) characterizes their statements and beliefs. If you knew me, you would know very clearly that I am thoroughly uninterested in the post-modern assumption that all ideas are equal and interchangeable. I understand that modernity has its issues when dealing with the subjective (yet very real) aspects of life, but post-modernist thinking today tends to swing the pendulum way too far in the opposite direction. Objective reality exists outside of our perception of it, and acting as though it doesn’t helps no one. This means that there are ideas which bear more merit than others, as they align more properly with truth.

That being said, there is a reason Christ instructed us to speak truth, in love. There is a reason why so much of the fruit of the spirit consists of attributes related to our treatment of others. The way we treat others matters, and at the moment, especially online, we treat others in a thoroughly uncharitable manner. Perhaps an example is in order.

A few weeks ago a well known Twitch streamer known as Pokimane released a short video talking about her interest in celibacy (something I personally practice, something the church advocates for, and something that is truly in line with God’s design for humanity, by the way), and to say the responses lacked charity would be a rather egregious understatement. The comments on twitter were nothing short of deplorable, calling her every manner of insult in the book, but they all shared one simple thing in common; every one of them made far sweeping assumptions about her, regarding things they could never actually know about her, and used those assumptions to characterize her in the most negative way possible. Put simply, every one of these folks lied, to themselves, and to each other, and used those lies as fuel to attack her.

This is true, even if the things they assumed were true. Why? Because none of them have any actual clue what they are talking about. It is entirely reasonable to assume she has been acting in this manner for some time, and even if she hasn’t, this sort of rhetoric is still rooted in falsehoods. Even if she had been sleeping with half of Los Angeles, the people calling her a whore would still be in the wrong. Just because you guessed right doesn’t mean you weren’t lying when you said it.

This woman is not perfect, but in my estimation, she is among the most uncharitably treated people on the internet. There are countless other examples, of her doing or saying something rather innocuous, sometimes even outright positive (as in this case), and the internet lies about the situation and bullies her incessantly. Make no mistake, assuming things about people in this manner, and using those assumptions as the basis for a hateful comment, or video on the internet is evil. This is just bearing false witness against someone. It is a defiance of the ninth commandment. That’s all it is. I understand this won’t carry weight for many people, but let’s call a spade a spade.

So what is the alternative? It’s quite simple really; tell the truth. If you don’t know what the truth is, don’t make stuff up. Don’t make far reaching assumptions based on insufficient evidence. Don’t bully people on the internet (even if you don’t like them), rather critically examine things they actually say and do, and only worry about things you can actually verify. There is enough deception in our world today, we don’t need to contribute even further to false narratives. Each of us would do well to remember that we will all stand before God one day and be held to account for the things we said and did. That won’t be a comfortable conversation for any of us, but it will be made even more uncomfortable if we consistently practice lying about people to ourselves, and others.

Give each other the benefit of the doubt. Practice the golden rule; ‘Do unto others, as you would have them do unto you.’ Stop judging people without sufficient reason to, especially on the basis of a single headline, or a few comments on the internet. This is one practical way we can all change the world for the better, and it requires almost nothing from us.

title: Hell.
html:
Last week we discussed the definition of good, which I put forth as the harmony between action, purpose, and potential. Those actions which most properly align us with our purpose and potential (as defined by God, of course) are good. This week I wish to run the thought experiment in the opposite direction, and to its natural (or perhaps unnatural) end. There may be some truth to the idea that we damn ourselves to hell, and that in so doing, we desecrate the one thing inside ourselves that makes us truly human.

Thanks for reading my Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

What happens when we consistently and defiantly choose actions which oppose our potential? What are the consequences of such decisions? Well if I had to use one word, I would use the word hell. This may be for reasons that you do not expect however. Let me be clear, regarding hell, there is a punitive, retributive aspect. In a technical sense, the Bible teaches that God created hell for the purpose of imprisoning Satan and his fallen angels, and that it essentially serves a dual purpose as the place for humans who reject God to go.

That being said, today I wish not to focus on the legal/penitentiary aspects of hell, but rather the state which accompanies them. In other words, what characterizes this experience, and what leads to it? If a human being, designed in the very image of God (imago dei), were to use his free will to openly, repeatedly, and ultimately defy the one who made him, what would happen? C.S. Lewis poses an answer to this question in his work ‘The Problem of Pain’’;

“To enter heaven is to become more human than you ever succeeded in being in earth; to enter hell, is to be banished from humanity. What is cast (or casts itself) into hell is not a man: it is “remains”.” - C.S. Lewis1

What Lewis is getting at here is the idea that at the very core of human existence is the image of God. To forsake that image is to forsake being human. It is what we would call ‘subhuman’. The implication here is that human beings, by virtue of being rational, free agents, have the ability to reject that which we were made for. We are unique in this way, we can choose to sin, to reject our telos. The consequences of sin are not merely temporal, however, in that they invariably prevent us from properly fulfilling our potential as image bearers. As Lewis points out, hell is the residence of such ‘sub humans’, or as he calls them ‘remains’, a place for people who are a mere shadow of their former selves.

This aspect of hell, where image bearers of God desecrate the very thing that makes them human, therefore becoming something less than, is often overlooked. I believe this constitutes what the Bible calls ‘eternal death’ or ‘eternal punishment’, not an annihilationist ceasing to exist, but rather a destruction of the one thing that makes us recognizably human. The entity in question is not removed from existence per se, but rather devolved beyond recognition. This disfigurement results in someone who is no longer recognizably human, someone who has lost/destroyed the very fundamental image that they were created to bear. After all, how could one eternally reject God, but remain an image bearer of His?

In this vein, we can understand Hell as something akin to eternal conscious torment, in that it is eternal, conscious, and full of torment, but that those three are actually symptoms of one’s loss of self, and the subsequent mutilation of the image of God(C.S. Lewis’ “The Great Divorce” explores this idea more).

So how does one get to this point? I have come to understand the justification for hell by understanding the concept of recidivism. Recidivism is essentially just the relapse of criminal behavior by someone who has already served their sentence. My concern however, is an eternal focus on recidivism. It is often argued that God cannot be just, and still damn people to eternal hell for temporal sin. In other words, how could any eternal punishment be justified on the basis of non-eternal actions? The short answer is that I don’t think we are damned on the basis of merely temporal actions. I think God allows us to make our own choices, and that He has mercy on those who repent. I also think that there are some who will not repent, and instead simply keep re-offending. They will relapse into sin, they will do so without remorse, and without regard for the God who made them. They will eternally reject Him, perpetually sin, and in this sense, they are not in Hell for temporal actions, but rather for eternal, perpetually reoccurring ones. They are victims, not of an all powerful immoral monster, but rather of their own devices. This is what I call ‘Recidivistic Damnation’.

Another important thing to note; if this is true, then human beings are at least partially responsible. It’s still proper to talk about the role of God’s sovereignty with regards to hell, but this means that each of us individually has a role to play in our own eternal status. Exactly to what degree this is the case, remains a mystery (and perhaps a video for another day).

When we reject God, and His good and perfect will for our lives, we are doing something consequential. This is not just another choice we make among many, it has very real and serious implications. We are rejecting the very source of our being, and the right and proper intention behind it. It is to reject our humanity in favour of something less than, and doing so has consequences.

C.S. Lewis is famously quoted as saying ‘the doors of Hell are locked on the inside’, and he consistently poses this idea in his books on the topic. For C.S Lewis, the idea that humans are their own captors, is instrumental to understanding hell. I agree, but this distinction is not either or. Rather I believe that both human will, and God’s wrath poured out, work in conjunction to produce what we refer to as hell. Romans 1 is rather instrumental to understanding how humans reject God, stating essentially that they choose to live in rebellion, and eventually God exercises His wrath on the unrighteous by allowing them to wallow in the ‘due penalty for their error’.

This is the terrifying reality of Hell; humans choose it, God allows us to choose it, and ultimately it results in a loss of whatever connection to God we have, as well as the very image that makes us human.

1

Lewis, C. S.. (The Problem of Pain.)

title: Good.
html:
Last week I introduced the concept of ideas having both an origin and a direction. This is perhaps most easily demonstrable with the concept of good (and evil, although that is a discussion for another time). What do we mean when we call something good? Today I would like to post a response to that question. This script is thoroughly immersed in the Christian worldview, and subsequent ethical considerations flow forth from the basic understandings that the church has claimed universally throughout human history.

Thanks for reading Joshua's Substack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

What we call good is really the state within which an entity is operating most closely aligned with its telos (or purpose). That’s a mouthful. When is a chair a ‘good’ chair? When it operates the way it is supposed to. When is a surgeon a ‘good’ surgeon? When he operates the way he is supposed to. When is a human a ‘good’ human? When he operates the way he is supposed to, when he operates in line with his design.

This brings us to an immediate question; how do we define the telos of a given entity? We first must look to the origin of that entity, to its creator, to determine what it was made for. For human beings this creator is the most high God. Only He has authority to make claims regarding the intent behind our creation, and only He can make clear to what end we are pointing. This is an important distinction when discussing science vs faith. Science is important, and can do many things, but one thing it cannot do, is tell us why. We can look at fossil records, or stars in the sky, and figure out a great many things, but we cannot determine what each telos is from mere observation. Only the creator has the authority to tell us why things exist.

The good news (the gospel) is that He has. We exist to reflect(image), and glorify our creator. For humans, actions which align us most closely with that end goal, are actions that can be called ‘good’. Actions which pull us away, distract from, or otherwise compromise that goal, are ‘evil’. This will be a tough pill to swallow for many, but truth tends to be difficult to hear. The bad news is that we all fail to properly align ourselves with ‘good’ rather often. We are all fallen, sinful beings, who (for the time being) are imperfectly aligned with the highest good. We are out of sync with our creator. This disparity forms the basis for the necessity of Christ’s intervention. We are a failed experiment, and none of us are capable of rectifying that failure on our own. Someone else had to, someone with standing, and authority to do so.

So if the distinction between ‘good’ and ‘evil’ for humans is the distinction between aligning ourselves with our telos, or not, then we can begin to apply this principle to determine the morality of various actions. Does this action align with God’s intent for me? Well now we run into another road block, how does one determine God’s creative intent (telos) for humans (both broadly, and specifically). This is yet another post for another day, as it begins to touch on the origins of Christian morality and deontological ethical frameworks.

For now, TLDR; good actions constitute aligning oneself with one’s origin and purpose. Our origin and purpose are both intimately connected to our creator, therefore our creator is the only one with authority to make claims regarding our ‘good’ or lack thereof. This brings up another related idea however; doing good is really acting in the way we were always meant to, it means being the kind of thing that we were always supposed to be. Fulfilling our potential to the best of our ability, is actually the same thing as doing ‘good’. When thought of this way, the idea of good expands from a narrow oversimplified trolley-problem decision making, into a full, holistic potential-fulfilling way of life. Each individual decision becomes not an end in and of itself, but rather an opportunity to act in full accordance with one’s potential.

Will this action push me towards, or away from that which I was made for, from that which God designed me to be? How do I go about cultivating a lifestyle that most properly aligns myself with the highest things that God is moving me towards? The interesting thing about this discussion is that it also reforms our understanding of biblical commands, such as “love your neighbour” and “love your enemies”. Follow me here. If good is defined according to a harmony between action, purpose, and potential, then love is seeking that which harmonizes one’s action, purpose, and potential, and loving others involves pursuing that which harmonizes their action, purpose, and potential. This means that both love of self, and love of others looks significantly different than what we imagine it does in today’s world.

Our primary concern is not with their hedonistic pursuit of pleasure or preference. If love is our genuine goal, as commanded by Christ Himself, then our primary concern must be how we can help others more properly harmonize their actions, with their purpose, and their potential.

Our love for others is, oddly enough, incumbent upon our ability to push back, or fight against their sinful desire to prioritize the self over God, just as our love for self is incumbent upon our ability to push back against our own selfish desires. This is a scary realization, because it requires far more involvement and combat from us than our cultural milieu would have us believe.

Now the way we go about this is important. I use a lot of warrior symbolism as a matter of preference, but violence is not the solution most of the time (edge cases exist of course). That being said, an illustration may be of benefit here. If I were a bystander to a man about to do something incredibly evil to a woman, what would the ‘good’ thing be to do? Many theologians have argued in the past (and I think they’re right) that the best thing I could do in that moment is do everything possible (including killing him) to prevent him from committing that sin. Prudence and wisdom are obviously necessary in such a situation, but the idea is that preventing him from going through with it, even if he loses his life, is better overall, not just for his victim;

The best good you can give them is the good of stopping them from committing this terrible sin. This is an extreme example, but it draws out an important principle. When our enemies aim to do evil things to others, the best way to love them is to stop them.1

Preventing others from doing evil things is loving. We have forgotten this, and it is far past time we remember.

1

Baird, James. King of Kings: A Reformed Guide to Christian Government (p. 91). Founders Press. Kindle Edition.

title: Ideas.
html:
One thing that always stands out to me when I am talking with people who have been raised in the west is how few people understand that ideas come from somewhere, and conversely, lead somewhere. Perhaps it is a side effect of the common secular, syncretistic attitudes towards belief systems, or in other words, the current cultural value that claims there is no inconsistency between belief systems, and that adopting, or ‘integrating’ small pieces from various worldviews is completely unproblematic and perhaps even helpful. A closer examination of this worldview renders it moot rather quickly, but most people never critically examine their belief systems.

At some point in the west we began to convince ourselves that these syncretism’s had no consequences, that importing ideas (and people) from the far corners of the earth on mass was actually a good thing. It has become quite clear in recent years that this failed experiment is on its last legs. This is due to one simple fact; ideas have an origin, and ideas have consequences. The idea that all cultures are equally moral comes from somewhere, and it leads somewhere. This is important to realize because the ideas that have allowed us to succeed as a people are intimately interwoven in our history, and failing to recognize and be grateful for those ideas in the last 70 years or so has led us all down a dark path.

This is most clearly the case in the United States of America. At its founding, the US was a nation of protestant Christian peoples, organized according to Christian ideas and law based on those ideas, and living in harmony as such. Whether or not you want to call it a Christian nation or not is irrelevant, the facts remain as such. Nearly everyone participating in this new American experiment fit those qualifications. Some of the founders were deists, sure, but even they were thoroughly immersed in the Christian worldview. The ideas that led to the American founding were almost universally Christian ideas. They came from somewhere, and they were pointed towards something (namely Christ).

This is significant because in recent years we have divorced these ideas from their only logical source. Simply put, many of the ideas that you, reading this substack, have always understood to be true and good, only exist because of Jesus Christ. This remains true even if you do not believe it. These ideas work solely because they are rooted in the character of a good God, and His divine intention for us humans. Divorcing the ideas from their origin is what got us into this mess in the first place. We have treated ideas as independent and interchangeable, and allowed ourselves the fantasy that there exists no consequence for borrowing a few ideas from secularism from time to time (for example). We have also treated people who adhere to these differing ideas as though there is no difference between them, although that is a topic for another time.

This brings up an interesting point however; can we profit from adopting good ideas, whose origin we are in contention with. In other words, can one benefit from the prosperity afforded to a nation that teaches and uplifts good ideas, while also rejecting the God from whom those ideas flow forth? Yes and no. There is a very strong case to be made that you cannot have your cake and eat it too. Some may argue that a nation under God is nothing if its individual citizenry are not followers of Christ. I agree and disagree. I think a nation that aligns itself with goodness and truth will be better off than a nation which doesn’t, simply because goodness and truth naturally lead to prosperity in the long run. That being said, true Christianity is better than cultural Christianity. But to be fair, cultural Christianity is far better than whatever garbage we have now. At least it would be somewhat logically consistent. As it stands, many people greatly value certain Christian ideas, while simultaneously valuing ideas that are nothing less than satanic.

Abortion would be a good example of this. Folks who are in favour of abortion generally hold the idea that all people are valuable and of worth, they simply have convinced themselves that those in utero are not yet people. They also tend to be not Christians. This is interesting because the idea that all people are valuable and of worth, is a Christian idea. It came from somewhere, and it is pointed towards something. In other words, the folks who seem to be almost always in direct opposition to Christianity operate on the assumption that parts of it are true, without knowing. But they do this, while rejecting other Christian ideas, such as the value of human life (beginning at conception).

So why does any of this really matter? Is it really the end of the world that people live according to shopping cart worldviews, where they pick and choose beliefs as they please? It does, because ideas are not just ingredients on a shelf. They have an origin, and consequences, and they interact with and sometimes combat one another, and suggesting that syncretism actually makes any sense is to deny the very existence of truth. At the end of the day, half-truths are still just lies. Eve was deceived in the garden by a collection of half-truths, Satan loves to use truth, but truth distorted, just enough that it becomes a weapon.

Our human societies succeed to the degree to which they are properly pointed at that which is good, and that which is true (and that which is beautiful, but I digress). As long as we insist on arbitrating according to our own syncretism’s, instead of according to the fount of truth Himself, we will fail. We will fall. We will suffer. It’s time for a return to form. It’s time to return to a world where we acknowledge exactly where the ideas we value come from, and where they are going.

title: Welcome and Introductions
html:
Hello there,

My name is Joshua. Welcome to my Substack.

My background is in theology, so expect that to be the main focus of most of my musings.
